239.t: Norman Granz's Ellington tapes and the lost Carnegie Hall Black, Brown and Beige
239.s: Jones believes Granz will release more Ellington material and recalls the black-market Carnegie Hall tapes he lost in a fire.
239.ch: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
239.q: I don't know. He'll probably release it someway, because I went to his office one day. You know, I was doing a string date with Milt Jackson, and Norman had so much stuff on Duke that he'd gotten from Mercer that hadn't been released. So I imagine he's going to release all this stuff.

239.t: Belafonte's TV show with Ellington segments and pre-recorded piano
239.s: Jones wrote the Ellington segments for Harry Belafonte's TV special, recorded with Hank Jones, while Duke clowned on camera.
239.q: No, I don't think so. But -- and Duke liked it, you know. And then I did quite a bit of work with Harry Belafonte, and Ellington was -- I think we called it, "The Strolling '20s." It was a big TV show.

239.t: What drew Duke to Jones: a shared approach to writing
239.s: Willard asks why Duke collected Jones; he cannot pinpoint it beyond liking his playing and writing.
239.q: You know, Pat, it's awfully hard to -- he liked my playing, he liked my writing, and it's awfully hard to pinpoint it, you know? It's almost like you start drifting together.

239.t: Duke's velvet glove with an iron mitt
239.s: Jones and Willard agree Duke disciplined subtly, as Procope put it, and the men stayed because they loved him.
239.q: Yeah. But I believe that was one of the reasons those men stayed with him so long. There was a comfort about him. Because the guys loved him.

239.t: The band that did not speak off stage; Duke the politician
239.s: Willard and Jones remark that Ellington's men stayed distant yet played together, and Strayhorn says Duke never noticed a missing saxophonist.
239.q: No. No, not at all. I think it was -- I think it was the most unique outfit that I've ever seen, you know, as far as the personnel, as you were saying, you know, how they were very courteous to everybody that wasn't in the

239.t: Duke's call about My People and conducting in Chicago
239.s: Duke phoned from Canada to send Jones to conduct the second Ellington band and choir at McCormick Place in Chicago.
239.q: It's never quite direct, you know. So he says, "Hey, James, this is Eddie Ellington." I said, "Hi, Edward, how do you feel?" So he says, "I have some singers I want you to take a look at," and it was Lil Greenwood, Jimmy Grissom, Joya Sherrill (PHONETIC). When I wound up I was out of town. I was…

239.t: Adopting Duke as a father figure and declining to go on the road
239.s: Jones's father mailed him Ellington clippings at school; later he told Duke it was too late to join the band.
239.q: Well, you know, that can happen. Because I just adopted Duke as a father when I was a kid, and my father got crazy about the music so much he would always keep me posted where Duke was playing, or you know, when I was away in school, and what he did, he would send me the clippings and the publicity.

239.t: Ellington's clashes and Willie Smith's seating in the saxophone section
239.s: Jones explains that Ellington's harsh writing would unnerve him and that Willie Smith disliked being seated apart from the saxes.
239.ch: Stuff Smith Trio and New York
239.q: Well, the -- oh, the things with Johnny Hodges, the ballads, with Otto Hardwick, they're soothing. But when Ellington would start writing all those clashes, then

239.t: Writing Ella at Duke's Place and Norman Granz stealing Jones from Duke
239.s: Duke asked Jones to write with him for the Ella Fitzgerald album while Strayhorn was ill, but Granz hired him for Ella.
239.q: I was sitting home and he was out -- he was working out here on the West Coast at that point, and he says, 'I would like for you to come out and write some scores with me.' Just like that.

239.t: Belafonte and the Ella-Ellington special: Jones writes the strings
239.s: Jones wrote strings for Duke Ellington's augmented orchestra in a Burbank television show; Duke himself did not write for strings.
239.q: Oh, yeah. Well -- but I think Strayhorn was still back east at that time.

239.t: Tizol and Cat Anderson nearly fighting; Duke stirring things up for the music
239.s: Duke wrote tension chords, then walked away from fights, and used anger by making feuding players take solos.
239.q: Yeah, you know. I think it was Tizol and Cat Anderson or something like that. So I told Duke, I said, "I told you about writing those high tension chords."

239.t: Jazz Party trumpet section, Dizzy brought in for discipline and the two bass players
239.s: Duke called Dizzy in when his trumpet players were missing, and hired a second bassist because Ragland drank.
239.q: I think it was on, "Jazz Party," the record, "Jazz Party," that I was on with the band, Quentin Jackson, Butter as we called him, told me -- it was on some

239.t: The emancipation centennial show and the cast album after Kennedy's assassination
239.s: The show celebrated a century of Negro progress; the cast album was recorded after November 1963 with the same company.
239.q: Because after we finished the engagement in Chicago and the President was assassinated, we had to go back to do a cast album, you know, that was after November.

239.t: Walking into the Jazz Party session and Duke's "virgin takes"
239.s: Duke pulled Jones to the piano with the red light on; Jones also tells of freezing on the A Train intro on Ellington Is Forever.
239.q: And there were a whole lot of people there, and there was like a -- it was a party, people were having drinks, because if you remember, Ellington had a lot of tympany and things, you know, he had something else in mind.

239.t: The Sinatra session where Jones played "I Like the Sunrise"
239.s: At the 1967 Sinatra-Ellington session Jones, called by Jimmy Hamilton, walked in and played the one Ellington number.
239.q: we have a score on this?" (Laughter) You know. Because after I left I gave him the parts, you know. And he says, "Yeah, we've got a good score on it." It's just like somebody else had written it, you know. We didn't talk about who had done it, you know. And --

239.t: Writing for a new voice and Bill Berry's first nights in the band
239.s: Duke wrote for individual players and tested newcomers; Bill Berry found cigarette-burned parts and was told to find a note.
239.q: Yeah. Well, Bill Berry has a funny story. When he came in the band. Well, he wasn't used to these personalities, you know, so there were no trumpet parts for him and those that he saw had cigarette burnings all over them, you know, and Cat and the guys, they wouldn't say anything to him, so he said…

239.t: Ray Nance, Duke Ellington and loving the old man
239.s: Willard and Jones discuss Ray Nance's devotion to Duke Ellington and their sense that Duke was unlike anyone else.
239.q: Yeah. And I saw the other side of him, but I still loved him, you know? He had something.

239.t: Sonny Greer's tempo trouble and Duke's reply, "Greer is ill. Do you know a physician?"
239.s: At the Chicago Theater Greer's drinking ruined tempos behind Sarah Vaughan, and Duke deflected George Treadwell's complaint.
239.q: I remember an experience, we were working the Chicago Theater, and they had -- we used to have to do like six shows a day, which is a hard day. We'd do the shopping show, which was about noontime, you know, into the closing hours. And I was working with Sarah Vaughan at that point, and Sonny Greer…

239.t: Preparing My People: the band, principals and the three-week run
239.s: Jones recalls the all-star second band, dancers and singers assembled in two days, and the show that caught on by word of mouth.
239.q: Because we had -- well, he got guys like Louis Bellson and Joey Benjamin and Bill Berry and -- who else? On the plane Duke says, "I'm going to give you Russell Procope and I'll go and get Hilton Jefferson for the road band."

239.t: No comparison in art: Ellington versus Lunceford and Duke's skill at agitating
239.s: Jones agrees there should be no ranking of great bands, recalls arguing Duke versus Lunceford, and says Duke knew how to agitate his men.
239.q: No, no. I agree with him totally on that. Because after all, in the final analysis I think that all of these guys are first class, you know, and after you get up in a certain area, it's a matter of choice, you know, a

239.t: First records with the Ellington orchestra: Jazz Party and a Hodges date
239.s: They sort out whether Jazz Party in 1958 was Jones's first Ellington record, and another Hodges-led date.
239.q: Yeah. Because there was another time I worked for the Ellington Orchestra, but Johnny Hodges was the leader.

239.t: How Jones came to work with Ellington: Mercer's band
239.s: Duke phoned at odd hours with propositions; Jones's first writing was for Mercer Ellington's Decca band.
239.q: Oh, let's see. It's kind of hard to put that together. I have some hazy moments in my memory, but if anybody knows Ellington, how he can call you at two or three o'clock in the morning wherever you are, but he's wide awake.

239.t: Duke's lesson: why he never gave Jones a conductor's score
239.s: Duke told Jones that a live show demanded knowing the score because there is no re-recording.
239.q: I tell you what he did. He's never one lost for words, no matter what the situation is, you know, so he eventually made a reply, after I was walking around in shambles. He says, "Well, James, you know this is not like a recording date where you can go and re-record or patch over. You have to know…

239.t: Duke's physical temper: Ben Webster, Hodges against the wall and ashtrays at Cootie
239.s: Stories of union representatives at the Sherman Hotel, Duke holding Hodges against a wall and throwing ashtrays at Cootie Williams.
239.q: Well, one time I think they had a problem. It was in Chicago and they were working the Sherman Hotel, and you had to come off the stand in one wing or the other. It was something like a stage, you know, at intermission. And Ben kept standing in the wings and he wouldn't allow Duke to come off the…

239.t: Writing for the HRS label with Ellington sidemen and catching Duke's attention
239.s: Jones recorded as a leader and writer with Carney, Hardwick, Lawrence Brown and others, which brought him to Duke's notice.
239.ch: Follow-up questions, Bird and the Ellington sidemen
239.q: doing more playing then. But I'll tell you during that time where I was doing a lot of writing, on a little small label called HRS, and let's see, who did we have, Harry Carney, Otto Hardwick, Lawrence Brown, Shelley Manne, Billy Taylor the bass player.

239.t: Why Duke wrote clashing chords for the Basie session and avoided a band battle
239.s: Duke's tension chords were deliberate, and he kept the joint session from becoming a contest.
239.q: He did that on purpose, because Basie plays kind of pure, you know. There's a difference -- but they sound good playing it. It's just that the -- Ellington just wrote that way. And okay, now there was -- of course there's going to be some competitive feeling, even though Duke and Basie were tight.…

239.t: The Duke Ellington and Count Basie joint album
239.s: Jones tells how Columbia and Roulette teamed the two bands for one day, with Duke writing harsh clashes that left Basie's men soaked.
239.q: Let me see, I'm trying to find some high points to it. Okay. I'll give you a little background first. Roulette Records had recorded Louis Armstrong and Duke in Europe. Bob Thiele Field was instrumental, I think, in putting that together.

239.t: Paul Gonsalves falling off his chair in Las Vegas and on Italian television
239.s: Two stories of Paul Gonsalves tumbling on stage, including Duke's quip that he did not drink and the Italian TV show with Ella.
239.q: beautiful human beings I ever met, you know, as a person. And -- but I remember one time I was in Vegas with Nancy Wilson, and Duke was in the Sahara. We were working at the -- oh, I can't think of the name of the hotel. The Sands. So we went down to catch Duke's band after we finished our show,…

239.t: Duke's scores on paper, odd voicings and why studio writing loses personalities
239.s: Tom Whaley's copying, Duke putting the baritone in the middle, and Ella's arrangement sounding vanilla with another orchestra.
239.q: Yes, that's right. That's very true, because there was one time I was doing some things with Johnny Hodges, you know, with a small group, about eight or ten pieces, and Tom Whaley -- Duke was living next door to me, and Tom Whaley was living about, oh, maybe three blocks away, and Billy Strayhorn.…

239.t: Harry Carney: how Duke won over his parents and the father-son bond
239.s: Jones tells of Carney being taken on the road, a photo of young Carney at Eubie Blake's, and Eubie's 95th birthday.
239.q: And we could see it coming. Of course the band was much smaller at that point, but they still had as much -- that basic excitement was there.

239.t: Duke making drunk sidemen play, especially Ben Webster
239.s: Jones thinks Duke embarrassed players rather than firing them, and that Ben Webster wanted to fight him.
239.q: Well, I think that Duke, rather than giving a guy notice, he would make the guy embarass himself.

239.t: The four arrangements Jones wrote, Gerald Wilson's tune and Duke's last-minute habit
239.s: Jones wrote four pieces on the album; they discuss Gerald Wilson's tune credited to Duke and Duke's last-minute pressure.
239.q: No. Okay, he used 'Passion Flower,' which was Strayhorn's. It was already there. She sang it. She was able to sing it in the key that Johnny Hodges played it in. And then Duke did, 'Azure,' and I did, 'Calico Gown.' There was four things I did. I didn't do but four.

239.t: The state of Ellington's library and who can read his scores
239.s: Willard and Jones agree few people, such as Herbie Jones and John Sanders, can interpret the scattered Ellington band book.
239.q: Yeah, that's right. Herbie worked close with the old man.

239.t: Duke calling Jones a member of the musical family
239.s: Willard notes Duke identified Jones as family in Music Is My Mistress and often asked for him.
239.ch: Stuff Smith stories, Wes Montgomery and singers
239.q: Yeah. That was kind of him. You know, that's quite a credit.

239.t: Stan Kenton's "new minority" remark and Duke's "race riot" at the Graystone
239.s: After Kenton's remark about white players, Duke fired up his band before a Detroit battle of jazz; Jones doubts Kenton meant it that way.
239.q: He really knew how to agitate. Well, you know, it was some years back -- I hope this doesn't offend anybody -- but Stan Kenton -- the times I've been around Stan Kenton, he's been very nice to me, you know, a nice guy. But he made a statement. I think he just -- he didn't really mean it as what…

239.t: Turning down Ellington's Sacred Concert work and the nudist camp joke
239.s: Newly settled in Los Angeles, Jones declined to return east for the second Sacred Concert, with a story about Duke's Reno suite.
239.q: Yeah. And I had just moved out this way at that point, and my wife and I had gotten settled, had a nice apartment and everything, and to get established as a resident musician you can't keep going in and out of town.

239.t: Duke as an effects man: Chuck Connors's low notes and Toch on Wagner
239.s: Duke wrote bass trombone parts below the range; Jones relates it to Wagner's writing for strings.
239.q: Yeah, I think he was an effect man, and that's what attracted me to them quite a bit, because everybody else, when I was coming up, thought in terms of notes, but Duke had effects. There was one time he had a funny line. He'd -- you know, horns have different ranges, and the bass trombone player,…

70.t: Hearing Duke Ellington's Jungle Band in Cincinnati
70.s: Passing through from the Check and Double Check film, Ellington's small-sectioned band played all original tunes; Jackson lists the men and discusses the jungle sound.
70.ch: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
70.q: The only other band that I heard that impressed me was that same year when I was with Zack White. I heard Duke Ellington's band. They came to Cincinnati and they was on the way from California -- they had just made the picture 'Check and Doublecheck' with Amos and Andy -- and they only had five…

70.t: Waiting on unemployment and Duke's offer to replace Claude Jones
70.s: After Ellington returned from Europe he offered Jackson Claude Jones's chair; Jones was unhappy being made to play valve trombone.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: And when Duke came back from Europe, I called him and asked him did he want me in the band. And then he told me yes, he said, 'You're going to take Claude Jones' place.' And I said, 'Oh, gee, I didn't want to do that,' you know, because, gee whiz, I mean Claude, you know --

70.t: Joining Ellington at the Duke Ellington Club in Washington
70.s: He joined on October 21, 1948, at a short-lived Washington club; Tyree Glenn had joined over a year earlier.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: That's right, and it was a club they tried to open called the Duke Ellington Club. It didn't last long because they couldn't get a liquor license.

70.t: What Duke Ellington was to Jackson: psychologist and diplomat
70.s: Jackson calls Ellington a great psychologist who wrote parts knowing how each man would play them.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: Well, I feel about Duke Ellington -- Duke Ellington to me was one of the most amazing men that I have ever known in life. He was a great psychologist. He was a great diplomat.

70.t: Third trombone, a lead part, and the name Monsieur du Beurre
70.s: Jackson, a famous low-note player, found a lead passage in his third part; Duke said he heard him on it, and in Paris in 1950 called him Monsieur du Beurre.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: We had an arrangement in the book that -- I always played third because, like all the bands I've been in, everyone wanted to hear me play low notes. I had made a name around New York for playing low notes, "Get Butter to play third trombone," you know, --

70.t: Duke writing constantly, untitled parts and calling him Edward
70.s: Ellington wrote on buses and bandstands, passing out untitled pieces that grew chorus by chorus, which confused substitutes.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: That's right. It was his workshop. He could do with it what he wanted it to, and there was so many arrangements in that book that a lot of people didn't even get to hear, because he was always writing. We would be on the bus, he would be writing. We would be playing a job, and I'd look over there…

70.t: His relationship with Ellington and the two raises
70.s: Ellington talked quietly with Jackson, and when he tried to quit twice Duke kept him until he agreed to a raise, partly because Basie asked him to join.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: My relationship was beautiful with him. He loved trombones. He always loved trombones. And a lot of times he used to come and talk to me about quiet things. You know, things -- he asked my -- even -- I can't say he asked my advice. He would talk to me sometimes to see my reaction to different…

70.t: Band changes in fall 1950: Cat Anderson back, trumpets
70.s: Al Killian left and Cat Anderson returned; Francis Williams and Nelson Williams are sorted out.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: That was 1950, the fall of '50. Al Killian -- I mean, Cat came back in the band. And we also had a trumpet player, Nelson Williams, that had been in the band in Francis Williams' place.

70.t: The weird scene in the band: loners and non-talkers
70.s: Sections barely spoke; Ray Nance and Al Killian were loners, Shorty Baker liked everyone, the trombones were close.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: I got along with them beautiful. I'll get along with anybody. You know, Milt, just like I said before, if you live with love in your heart, it -- you know, people will know. I never had a minute's trouble with nobody.

70.t: The early 1940s Ellington trombone section Jackson could only envy
70.s: Jackson sat in Tizol's seat after hours at the Hurricane and Strand and lists the 1942-43 band he heard.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: That's right. No trombone player. I used to go up there to the Hurricane so I could even just sit in. When we played the Strand Theater I used to go out there after the last show so I could sit in Tizol's seat.

70.t: Duke's instruction not to play too pretty, and descriptive music
70.s: Duke told him the music was folklore; Jackson explains Ellington's black music, colors, and descriptive pieces.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: Then, you see, when I first came in the band, Duke told me, when I started to playing, he said, you know, he said, "Let's not play this too pretty." He said, "Tyree played a little bit too pretty." He said, "Let's not play this too pretty." He said, you know, "This is folklore."

70.t: 1951: Hodges leaves and Britt Woodman and Tizol arrive
70.s: Hodges, Greer and Lawrence Brown left to form Hodges's band in 1951; Britt Woodman came from Los Angeles and Claude Jones briefly returned.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: And that's what made the band so fantastic. It was just -- any, any -- every band while I was there, even when they changed men -- you know, in 1951, we went through a big change in the band.

70.t: Duke tearing apart arrangements for continuity
70.s: Henderson wrote commercially despite playing bebop, and Duke reworked any arrangement, jumping between letters; he told Jackson he didn't like the continuity.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: Rick made a couple of good arrangements, and it was a funny thing, you know. Rick Henderson played one way but he wrote another. Now, he played be-bop saxophone to me but his writing was rather on the commercial side, you know, and to me it was an oddity. But he made good arrangements, but I don't…

70.t: Billy Strayhorn and Ellington's writing marriage
70.s: Jackson calls Strayhorn and Ellington the greatest musical marriage; Strayhorn was tender, and arrangements were passed between them so you couldn't tell who wrote what.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: Yeah, just like I asked Billy Strayhorn once about -- I heard the saxophone section play a thing and he had Harry Carney playing up above the tenor for a few bars and then, all at once, he dropped him below the tenor, you know, back down on the bottom. I said, "Sweet Pea," I said, "I heard what you…

70.t: How Strayhorn joined in 1939 and the tunes he wrote
70.s: Ellington got Strayhorn in Pittsburgh in 1939; he wrote Chelsea Bridge, Passion Flower, Take the A Train and Lush Life.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: He got Strayhorn in Pittsburgh. Strayhorn wanted to write for the band and he brought some things to Duke and Duke liked it. He liked it and he kept Strayhorn with him and Strayhorn was a big help to him later on. Strayhorn arranged a lot of hits. He wrote a lot of hit tunes in that band: 'Chelsea…

70.t: Lush Life as a controversial lyric
70.s: Jackson and Hinton discuss the lyrics of Lush Life about gay spots as daring for its time, and also racy titles in Ellington's book.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: Oh, so far ahead. And, of course, I can tell you too, there was some titles on some of the music in that book that you better not put on a record.

70.t: Strayhorn as a gentleman who never made himself obvious
70.s: Hinton wonders whether gay admirers know Strayhorn; Jackson says he was a perfect gentleman beloved by all, nicknamed Sweet Pea by Ben Webster.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: Well, I think, to me, he was so far ahead of the average person, gay or not gay, intellectually, till they just -- I don't think they really realized or picked up on it really.

70.t: The 1955 Flushing Meadows water show without Ellington's regulars
70.s: Because many regulars lacked New York union cards, outside players filled in at the water and ice show, and Jackson played first trombone.
70.ch: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
70.q: Now, the band stayed like that until we got to -- we played the water show in 1955. We played the water show out in Flushing Meadows. That's where they had the water show during the World's Fair both in the thirties and this last World's Fair. And we played a combination water show and ice show…

70.t: The Ellington band is a disease; Duke and Basie as friends
70.s: Jackson says anyone who played in the band can't forget it; Basie called Duke the master, and other bands' music felt mediocre afterward.
70.ch: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
70.q: Oh, I'll never forget him as long as I live. And I tell you something else about the Duke Ellington band. That band, if you've ever been in it, is a disease. I don't care who you play with, who you have played -- or who you have played after, you'll never forget it.

70.t: Tyree returns for the Masterpieces by Ellington album
70.s: Tyree Glenn only came back to record Masterpieces by Ellington with Mood Indigo and Sophisticated Lady, then returned to gigging and the Ted Steele show.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: He just stayed in New York and got to gigging around New York and everything and that was right before that he got the Ted Steele show, you see. And he was really doing -- he was doing all right for himself. He wasn't hurting at all.

70.t: No one like Duke; Thad Jones as today's arranger
70.s: Jackson says there will be no one like Ellington and names Thad Jones as today's greatest arranger.
70.ch: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
70.q: Now, we've got an arranger now to me that is -- as far as making arrangements to me is the greatest arranger today, as far as I'm concerned, in jazz music, that comes almost up to that, and that is Thad Jones.

70.t: Ellington at the piano and humming when the band cooked
70.s: Ellington hummed and hit chords behind soloists when he was pleased, and Jackson says he was a great accompanist who knew where you were.
70.ch: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
70.q: They would fire up like nothing you ever heard in your life. And Duke would sit there and whenever you could see him with that frown on his face and he would start to humming that one tone, the band was knocking him out then and he was very pleased.

70.t: The Oasis, Charlie Smith, and Louie Bellson, Tizol and Willie Smith arriving
70.s: On the road the replacements failed, until in Omaha Bellson, Tizol and Willie Smith joined and the band tightened.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: So we went on to the Oasis, the club in Frisco -- and, by the way, when Johnny left we sent to Kansas City and got one of the Douglas brothers. They were saxophone players in Kansas City, good saxophone players, but it wasn't really what Duke wanted.

70.t: Newport Jazz Festival 1956 and Paul Gonsalves's 27 choruses
70.s: At Newport 10,000 people went wild during Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue; George Wein told Duke to stop but Duke played on.
70.ch: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
70.q: Because this band was so fantastic. I want to talk about the concert we did at Newport in '56 which to me was history. We had 10,000 people there and I never seen people go crazy. That was the night that we did "Diminuendo and Crescendo in Blue and Paul Gonsalves went out there and played 27…

70.t: How Duke wrote for individual players
70.s: Ellington gave each man particular notes in chords and made new arrangements when personnel changed; he used Hamilton, Procope and Carney expertly.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: And I noticed how he would use different musicians in the band. He would take your sound and use it. He would give you certain notes and certain chords, like he would give me certain notes in a chord that he wouldn't give Lawrence or give Tyree or even Britt Woodman or John Sanders, and that's the…

70.t: And His Mother Called Him Bill and Strayhorn's Blood Count
70.s: Jackson A&R'd the Strayhorn tribute date because he knew all the music, and recalls Blood Count as Strayhorn's last piece, played by Hodges.
70.ch: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
70.q: I knew where the saxophones was supposed to be brought up, I knew where the solos were. So he told me, he called me and said, you know, because at that time I wasn't playing, and he said, "I want you to come and A and R

70.t: Outswinging Stan Kenton at the Graystone
70.s: Woodyard rallied the band to put the pots on, and Ellington's band swung all night while Kenton's men stood astounded.
70.ch: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
70.q: There's some beautiful stories about that band, too. We played the Graystone with Stan Kenton and that band swung all night long. They took us out of the ballroom and put us in the garden and the people were screaming when we finished there. And Stan asked his band to leave and they wouldn't leave.…

70.t: Oscar Pettiford sits in at Stony Brook
70.s: Pettiford with his amplified bass sat in for Woode and drove Paul Gonsalves to 36 choruses; Woodyard told Jackson how Oscar laid it in your lap.
70.ch: Ellington's later years and Quincy Jones
70.q: Yeah. Jimmy Woody was the bass player. And there was a couple of times that Oscar come back and played in Jimmy Woody's place, too, out there in Long Island. Now, what's that place out there, on the hill out there? I know you have played out there. Stony Brook.

30.q: I think -- No -- I think -- not playing, not by a longshot. His talents, I mean, he was a creative man to begin with and he had marvelous ideas and which I give him a lot of credit because if he heard something, like I said, if I was playing a solo or something -- you know, like a little jazz thing…

30.t: Duke never fired anyone, he made them quit
30.s: Bigard says Duke made people so miserable they quit; he could not do it to Bubber Miley or Otto Hardwick, hounded Freddie Guy out, and eventually fired Sonny Greer.
30.q: That's true, but he made it so miserable. If he wanted somebody to leave, he made them so miserable that if they had any kind of pride within themselves, that they would just quit, and that would satisfy his ego and it kept his record clear that he's never fired anybody.

30.t: Duke's bodyguards Weak Knees and Jonesy
30.s: Bigard calls Duke a coward who had a Washington bodyguard called Weak Knees and a valet, Jonesy, and once tricked Bigard into breakfast as his protection.
30.q: And Duke was a coward. He'd do all his dirty work and he'd have a guy, like, in Washington called "Weak Knees," a bad guy, and he'd have him protecting him all the time when he was in Washington.

30.t: Duke composing the Cotton Club show on the spot and Calloway's lost bet
30.s: Duke never wrote introductions or endings down; he gave each man his notes and rhythm at rehearsal, and Cab Calloway lost a bet with Herman Stark that the show would not open on time.
30.q: You know, I was thinking, since I saw you last, at the Cotton Club -- you know, Duke used to write a lot of music for the show and it was always a peculiar thing about him, that he'd never make an introduction to the number, whatever, the girls were going to dance, or an ending. So Calloway used to…

30.t: Duke's snubs of Sonny Greer and Ray Nance on the concert night
30.s: Duke brushed off Sonny Greer, introduced Bigard briefly and played the tune too slowly, and never called Ray Nance from the wings.
30.q: So when the curtain went up for the concert, Sonny was downstairs. They called me down. I came down and I sat. And Duke was announcing. So all of a sudden he called, "Here's the great Greer." And that's all. The boy hadn't gotten off the drums yet. Sonny had to climb up on that stage to get on the…

30.t: Duke's and Sonny Greer's memory for faces and tunes
30.s: Bigard says Duke had a phenomenal memory and so could Sonny Greer, who would remind him who visitors at the Cotton Club were.
30.q: And you're talking about a man that can remember tunes of the past years and people of the past years. He had that memory. He was phenomenal. I've never seen anybody like that.

30.t: Harry Carney's devotion and Duke's family
30.s: Willard says Carney treated Duke like a father; Bigard says Duke treated his own son badly, favoured his sister Ruth, and adored his mother.
30.q: Yeah, with the mother and the father and Duke, because anything his mother would say, that was it, because he was madly in love with his mother, which is wonderful.

30.t: More of Duke's late cruelties: Norris Turney and Tony Watkins
30.s: Willard tells how Duke doubled the tempo behind Norris Turney until he quit and left Tony Watkins waiting in the wings of a television show; Bigard agrees he got terrible.

30.t: The time Bigard nearly beat Duke
30.s: Duke interfered in Bigard's love life; Bigard grabbed him by the neck before Cootie caught his arm, and he thinks Tizol once wanted to cut Duke.
30.q: Show somebody how to do, what to do, and what not to. You see, I'm a man. I'm like you. I don't tell you what to do. And one word led to another and I just grabbed him and I was going to whack him, and one of the guys -- I

30.s: Duke's arrangements left a bare space marked 'solo' of eight or sixteen bars, with no time to settle in on an original tune.

31.t: Meeting Duke Ellington in 1922 and his rise to the Cotton Club
31.s: Whaley meets Duke at Robinson's Restaurant, tells how Duke took over Elmer Snowden's band from Sonny Greer, and describes Hardwick, Carney and Bubber Miley.
31.ch: Coming up in New York and Harlem theatres
31.q: That was in 1922 and I was sitting down there playing the piano and somebody says there's Duke Ellington, well, I had heard about him but I didn't know him so I kept on playing and he come over, and they introduced me to him. He was down at the Kit Kat -- no, what is that club downtown.

31.t: Copying for Duke and Juan Tizol's refusal
31.s: Whaley says too much copying ruined his eyes, and Hinton calls him the one copyist who could read Duke's handwriting, after Tizol.
31.ch: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
31.q: No. I know what it was. Too much work. That's strain. I used to sit in Duke's home and he'd sit there writing and then we'd go down to the rehearsal hall where they're going to record and I would start copying it and by the time he had finished one number I had another number there ready for him.

31.t: Duke's pencil and trust between them
31.s: Whaley describes Duke erasing and changing notes on scores, and says they trusted each other completely.
31.ch: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
31.q: I never knew anything about that. But I know Duke would make an arrangement and he'd have this pencil with an eraser on it and he'd stand up there and erasing

31.t: How Duke built up a performance after intermission
31.s: Hinton and Whaley describe Carney's reliability and Duke calling the band back with 'A Train', 'Mood Indigo' and 'Satin Doll'.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: The "A Train", see, and then go from the A Train he would go into a number for probably Cootie, see, and from then he would give a preparation for 'Mood Indigo' and that's three guys would come out and then he would go into Harry Carney on "Sophisticated Lady" and from Harry he would go into "Satin…

31.t: Starting to copy for Duke in 1940
31.s: After the theatre closed in 1940 Duke wanted a copyist, and in 1942 in Hollywood Whaley copied 'Black, Brown and Beige'.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: In 1940, you know, I was at the theatre and the girls in 1940, they wanted more money and the man wouldn't give them any more money so they closed them up and closed my job out also, so I was hanging around, so I don't know how, but I got in contact with Duke or Duke got in contact with me and…

31.t: Duke's show 'My People' in Chicago and Detroit
31.s: He describes 'My People', the education of the Negro through music, which he copied, and the huge crowds in Detroit.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: and I said, hey, what are you going to do with this, and he said nothing, but in 1963 he went to Chicago and included -- he made My People, that was the show and in that show was 'Black, Brown and Beige.' He had the people coming from the pit, they were in rags, my people, our people in rags coming…

31.s: They agree it was the greatest band, naming Ray Nance, Tricky Sam, Hamilton, Rex Stewart and Ben, and Whaley praises their interpretation.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: Yeah, to me that was a great band, see. Because the guys understood, you know, and they would play and bend a note, they could bend a note instead of playing it just as a quarter note or half note or eighth note, they would bend it and play it this way. Give it some color and everything.…

31.t: Billy Strayhorn and his Monday visits
31.s: He says he could not tell where Duke ended and Strayhorn began, and Strayhorn visited every Monday for a beer.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: Oh, that was beautiful. Strayhorn was -- he could -- Duke could start something and he would end it, and you'd never know whether Duke started or stopped or Strayhorn started.

31.t: 'Lush Life' and Strayhorn's nickname Sweet Pea
31.s: They talk about the difficult changes of 'Lush Life', and that no one played it like Strayhorn.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: The thing that Billy wrote and I never learned was that thing that Duke played. And I was talking about it the other day.

31.t: Dating his friendship with Duke Ellington
31.s: Whaley fumbles whether he met Duke at the Kentucky Club in 1922 or about 1925, and that he followed Duke to the Cotton Club in 1927.
31.ch: Working with Duke and final reflections
31.q: And well, it wasn't '22. Yeah, I met Duke right after I came -- no, it must have been later. It was about, say, '25. Because it was right before Small's opened up on 135th Street, and the Savoy Ballroom, it was right before then that I met Duke -- but it was at the Robinson Restaurant, see, and I…

31.t: Starting to copy for Duke after the Apollo closed
31.s: Whaley lost his Apollo job in 1940, Duke called wanting a copyist, and Duke trusted him to change parts that sounded wrong.
31.ch: Working with Duke and final reflections
31.q: So in '40, Duke called me and I thought I was going to be an arranger, see, and he wanted a copyist. I said okay, I'd copy.

31.t: 'Black, Brown and Beige', 'Come Sunday' and the Chicago show
31.s: Whaley orchestrated 'Come Sunday' and 'Black, Brown and Beige' in Hollywood, and describes the 1963 Chicago show with Alvin Ailey and the rising pit.
31.ch: Working with Duke and final reflections
31.q: You know, I was in Los Angeles, Hollywood when we made 'Black, Brown & Beige,' and this thing was -- you know, it stuck in my mind -- da, da, da, da, That's a number that Johnny Hodges made famous.

31.t: Mercer Ellington, Duke's estate and Duke's visit before his hospital stay
31.s: Whaley thinks the money changed Mercer, that Mercer's book on his father was wrong, and that Duke visited him with $100 and steaks before hospital.
31.ch: Working with Duke and final reflections
31.q: I don't know, Mercer went crazy, I think; he went off his lid when he got all this money from Duke. You know, Duke had left around $200,000, see. Something like that.

31.s: Whaley tells of answering Duke's mail, copying without discussion, and Duke reversing the order of sections.
31.ch: Apollo years, Eubie Blake and failing eyesight
31.q: : Oh, yes, I used to answer all his mail and sometimes I'd get a letter, somebody would say hey, Duke, we got some girls here, come on. Shall I call them up. Yeah, call them up. And I remember in Detroit, Michigan, we had Al, what's his name, the manager. John used to --he used to hang around and…

31.t: Sacred concerts, conducting at Harvard and the first at Grace Cathedral
31.s: Whaley tells how he rehearsed and conducted the choir at Harvard and Texas, and dates the first Sacred Concert in San Francisco.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: I could see Duke progressing every year it was something different and when he came into the sacred concert music, ah, that was my field. Oh, I loved --

31.t: Duke head over heels in music, and Vodery and Luther Henderson
31.s: Whaley sums up Duke as head over heels in music, praises Vodery writing amid noise, and recalls Luther Henderson watching him orchestrate at the Lafayette.
31.ch: Working with Duke and final reflections
31.q: Anyway, I thought Bill Vodery was great, stand up there and write with all that going on. Well, I did it myself at the Lafayette Theatre; I sat there and I used to orchestrate and Luther Henderson, he says he saw me doing that -- this was before Luther got big, you

31.t: Chairman of the Board of Duke's band
31.s: Whaley explains how he became Duke's 'Chairman of the Board' by handling Duke's mail and sending Christmas money to relatives.
31.ch: Working with Duke and final reflections
31.q: Well, see, when I first went into the band, I used to take all of his mail and read it and if he had anything important, I used to tell him.

31.t: Ben Webster and Otto Hardwick in Duke's band
31.s: He describes Ben Webster drinking and rehearsing one thing and playing another, and Hardwick and Carney controlling the band's dynamics.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: I got along with all of them. Ben Webster, he used to say, don't wake up Tom. Ben would have his beer and have a bottle and he'd sit there and drink all the time and he would get high but you wouldn't know it, see, he would get them sleepy eyes and go to sleep. The band --

31.t: Tricky Sam Nanton and Sam Woodyard
31.s: Whaley tells of Tricky Sam's death on tour and his plunger work, and of Woodyard being a loner.
31.ch: Suntaug Lake Inn and Duke Ellington's band
31.q: Yeah, he died while we was in -- up there in -- one of those shows, one of those roads coming from San Francisco. We had been out all night, see and I said to Tricky, I'm going on to bed, so he said all right and got up and I called him and he didn't answer, so it's time to go to the show and still…

409.t: Johnny Hodges tells Duke about Cootie
409.s: Johnny Hodges, once with Chick Webb, recommended Cootie to Duke after Bubber Miley was fired; Cootie had thought the Ellington band comedy music.
409.q: Yeah. He was a wonderful guy. And after he told Duke about me, after Duke fired Bubber Miley, he said, "Why don't you get Cootie?", Johnny told him. So I never played no music like that.

409.t: Why Duke fired Bubber Miley, and Duke's hands-off style
409.s: Bubber was the only man Duke fired, for being absent when big shots came; Duke never told Cootie what to play.
409.q: The reason why he fired Bubber Miley was every time someone big shot come up to listen to the band, there wasn't no Bubber Miley. And he had the whole band built around Bubber Miley.

409.t: Duke's hands-off management and never firing anyone
409.s: Duke gave men freedom, never bothered anyone and fired no one, even when Paul Gonsalves or Willie could have been.
409.q: Yeah. Well, he never bothered a man. You would come in there, and you would just go to work. And that's all. He never said nothing to you, never speak to you. 'Hey', he'd say. That's all. Never bothered nobody.

409.t: Strayhorn's work habits compared with Duke's
409.s: Duke wrote continually; Strayhorn wrote only on assignment and liked to party and jam.
409.q: No, no. You're absolutely right. Strayhorn was a young boy, you know. He wasn't no stay in like Duke, and sit at no piano all day and all night, just continuously, day in and day out, you know, like that. No. He wasn't going to do that. He used to like to party and ball.

409.t: Strayhorn joining the band and writing for Johnny Hodges
409.s: Strayhorn was respected once they played his music; his only band number was A Train, the rest written with and for Hodges.
409.q: Oh, well, yeah. Yeah. They had a lot of respect for him. They knew. They knew who he was.

409.t: Duke's funeral and why Cootie stayed with Mercer
409.s: The funeral recalled the Sacred Concert; Cootie calls Duke the greatest man he met and stayed on to help Mercer.
409.q: Yeah. I went out with the band for that reason, the main reason, on account of Duke. Because I thought he needed me, and he really needed me at that time.

409.t: The Ellington band after Cootie and Johnny left
409.s: They discuss the 1940 band, the last session Concerto for Cootie, Ben Webster and who left next.
409.ch: Leaving Duke and the Goodman sextet
409.q: Yeah, the last session -- no. The last session I made was "Concerto for Cootie". I remember that.

409.t: New men left to find their parts
409.s: New saxophone players had no one to show them the unwritten parts and sat lost until Harry Carney or others helped; Ben Webster was liked.
409.q: In the later days. Because a guy would come in the saxophone section, a new man come in there, and he'd just be setting there. A guy wouldn't tell him what he'd be playing next or nothing. He'd just be sitting there. He'd be lost. By the time he'd be getting into the number, he'd be looking for the…

409.t: Strayhorn's death and Duke giving credit
409.s: Strayhorn died in 1967 after sending Blood Count; Cootie agrees Duke always gave Billy credit.
409.q: Yeah. He did. He really minded.

409.t: Duke asks him to come back
409.s: Duke called twice asking him to return, saying he only had to sit there; Cootie went back for him alone.
409.q: But during the period of time they were over there, Duke called me. He says, -- called me twice, I think. He says, "Are you ready to come back to go to work?" I said, "No, man. I ain't thinking about working no more." He said, "Ah, don't do that, man." He said, "I miss you so much." He said, "Come…

409.t: Johnny Hodges' death and his relationship with Duke
409.s: Hodges' death in 1970 was a blow; Cootie says he and Duke were very close.
409.q: That was a very close relationship there, between those two. Always, you know. Johnny was real close to him, you know. They was real tight.

409.t: Mercer Ellington and Johnny Hodges' own band
409.s: Dance and Cootie sort out Mercer's credits and Hodges leaving to lead a band with Strayhorn.
409.q: Well, the thing sounds like Johnny Hodges to me.

409.s: Paul was great when straight; Duke called Paul's hardest number when he was stoned or sleeping and used Harold Ashby as a replacement.
409.q: Oh, Paul was a great saxophone player. When And Paul was straight, I think he was one of the greatest tenor

409.t: Rejoining Duke's band after twenty-three years
409.s: He told Harry Carney he was ready and found it felt like being back home.
409.q: Uh-huh. It felt fine. Felt like I was back home.

409.s: Carney joined 1927, Hodges 1928, Cootie 1929; Cootie says Sonny Greer fit the band as no one else could, and liked Louis Bellson.
409.q: He and Barney was from New Orleans, and they had that New Orleans thing going, you know. So that's the reason why they would be over there talking that half Creole stuff, and we didn't like that so much.

409.t: Parts given out orally on record dates; no written bass part
409.s: On sessions Duke dictated notes at the piano; he never wrote a bass part until later years.
409.q: Well, on a record session, then, you'd go on a record session, he'd just give out notes, sit there at the piano and say, 'You play this,' you know, different guys. 'Your part is this, your part is that.' So it never was written out.

409.t: Policing the Ellington band when Duke would not
409.s: In Duke's band Cootie hollered at Hodges and Bigard if they played wrong or fooled around, since Duke never spoke.
409.q: Yeah. If Johnny or Barney or any of them were in an argument, wasn't playing the music right, I'd holler at them. Because Duke would never say nothing to them. I'd be the one that had taken over that spot.

93.t: Dancing to Ellington outside Lucille Achet's shop and a lifetime contract offer
93.s: Dancing outside the record shop to Ellington's Ring Them Bells brings customers in; the owner offers to manage him on a lifetime contract and take him to New York.
93.q: So I continued to do this. In the meantime I got back to the 81 Theater, to this lady's record shop, Miss Lucille Achet. That was George Roby's daughter-in-law. And he was a fight promoter, and he had Obey Bearcat Walker and a couple of more fighters. Obey was a heavyweight, and the others was --…

93.t: Ellington's package of dance acts and talent scouts
93.s: Ellington carried varied dance acts like the Five Blazes and Chuck and Chuckles, which inspired his music and exposed them to Hollywood talent scouts.
93.q: Yes, yes. Well, he actually introduced these shows -- I mean these acts in his shows on his tours or appearances for the purpose of that, you see. Because you would never know how many talent scouts would be in an audience or who they were from or who they were representing. Of course, like he --

93.t: What it was like dancing with Duke Ellington
93.s: Green calls it the greatest experience; he recalls the Mao Brothers, Snake-Hips Tucker numbers, Ellington inheriting the Cotton Pickers, and Ellington's stature with visiting royalty.
93.q: Oh, I guess -- I don't know if it was ever explained, but I think it's the greatest think anyone could have experienced because -- it was all truth, I would say. Anyone who wanted to be anything for theirself or the audiences, see -- see, fan clubs were very popular, see. They were also discovering…

93.t: Opening the Ellington show with Black and Tan Fantasy
93.s: Green describes the show opening with the theme Black and Tan Fantasy, then hits like Sentimental Mood and Prelude to a Kiss before the first act.
93.q: Well, it would open with the Duke Ellington Band theme song, which was at that time 'Black and Tan Fantasy.' Then they would play 'Sentimental Mood' (sic) 'Prelude to a

93.t: The Mao Brothers and the richness of Ellington's band
93.s: Green says the Mao Brothers opened as jazz tappers and claims Ellington's band had the richest sound, recalling the Cotton Club moving downtown to the Zanzibar.
93.q: Yes. They was known as the Terrific Tappers, you know, the Mao Brothers. Then, of course, there was some more of the band music, you see.

93.t: Rest of the Ellington show: Harry Richman, Mills Brothers, Herb Jeffries
93.s: Green recounts the order of acts, with Richman, Mills and Mills, Herb Jeffries singing Prelude to a Kiss, then dancers; Ellington was rarely in America for long.
93.q: Well, that's it. He was in the show also -- Harry Richmond, see. He came on after the Mao Brothers, you see. Then after he was on there, then Mills and Mills -- they

93.t: Ellington calls himself Pop and enjoys Chuckles
93.s: Chuckles' vibraphone and operatic scat pleased Ellington; Green tells him his partner is a big fan and Ellington says call me Pop.
93.q: It was very classy, very classy. That's why I say rich, you know, enriching. See, Duke Ellington's appearances, you know, on these tours -- because I mean America couldn't keep this man very long -- he was in such great demand with that orchestra, see. I mean, there was other countries that wanted…

93.t: Ellington adopted them; the separation dance and the baptizing walk
93.s: Ellington kind of adopted the pair; Green describes their separation dance to Scatting at the Kit Kat and introduces his baptizing walk.
93.q: No, no, no. It was just doing my dancing. I was tap dancing in my act, you see, 'Scatting at the Kit Kat.' See, now, he was already the composer of this melody, see. But Chuck and Chuckles had -- we had a separtion tap dance we did. Some would call it competitive, you know, or playing or…

93.t: Demonstrating the baptizing walk, a tribute to Ellington and Bubbles
93.s: Green says he wanted to be a stunt man, then performs his tap walk to Take the A Train as a courtesy to Ellington, from Bubbles' step to the diggings.
93.q: Well, I tried to eventually to become a stunt man and I was hoping someday to see where did they go to school. Where do -- where is the stuntman's school? That was always a, you know, a thinking I had. Where do they -- who are some of the stuntmen's teachers. I mean, what's their names? And, so, I…

93.t: Starting on the Ellington charter tour at the William Penn Theater
93.s: Asked for one big-band experience, Green picks the Duke Ellington charter beginning in Pittsburgh, with the Berry Brothers on the bill.
93.q: Well, the most important was the Duke Ellington one, yousee, because that was a charter. We had to go up into -- outside of this town, I think it's called -- oh,

93.t: Walking cramp, kick cramp and Duke Ellington's Main Stem
93.s: Green restates the cramps, describes his walks around Harlem and Seventh Avenue as the main stem, and hearing Ellington's Main Stem at Bubbles' house.
93.q: Now, as I was saying, we were speaking about the walking cramp and the kick cramp, and the difference in the qualities. (Unintelligible) the kick cramp was much richer than the walking cramp, which is absolutely true. Because that is so. The walking cramp is on one foot, and the kicking cramp is…

93.t: Sacko and Ina Ray Hutton on the Ellington show
93.s: Green says dancers brought a thrilling tumbling jazz tap called sacko, and tells of Patterson and Jackson replacing the Berry Brothers and Ina Ray Hutton singing.
93.q: But the dancers done all right. They introduced sacko -- they brought that to the profession. Called sacko -- that's handling it down from tap dancing -- sacko.

93.t: Duke Ellington's Breaking in a Pair of Shoes
93.s: Ellington gave Chuck and Chuckles the song Breaking in a Pair of Shoes; they filled in for Tip, Tap and Toe on an Ellington tour, with one singing while the other danced.
93.q: Oh, my goodness. Well, if there's been some people writing songs, they all come by Duke Ellington especially. He composed a song, him and one of his colleagues, they composed a song called, "Breaking in A Pair of Shoes". And he gave that to Chuck and Chuckles as a present, you see. We pinch hitted…

93.t: Being held over at the Penn Theater and the big band era
93.s: Green says this was the first time he was held over; he rambles on repeat performances, talent scouts, fan clubs, and Whiteman introducing Ellington as King of Jazz.
93.q: Well, I think we got held over there, you see. We got held over at this place, see. That's the Penn Theater, see. Now, that's the first experience that I ever had of being held over. Even with Buck and Bubbles, I mean, we wasn't like in no held-over shows, but we had been in the -- you know, like…

93.t: Big time, Desi Arnaz's orchestra and Fred MacMurray
93.s: Green drifts to the idea of big time and a Philadelphia show with Desi Arnaz's orchestra, a blond violinist and saxophonist Fred MacMurray being discovered.
93.q: Yes, I believe I can. It's what we call display window, and there was -- they were doing first, see, having a first -- one of a kind, like that, and hoping that it had enough appeal -- audience appeal, to become popular. You see, the public at large -- they didn't know what to expect, you know,…

16.t: Joining Ellington: first arrangements before the Navy and later work
16.s: He wrote four arrangements, including Indiana, before reporting to the Navy; he worked with Ellington from 1943 until his death in 1970.
16.q: How did that happen … let's see. I guess it just happened that, I guess I was pretty obvious about wanting to write something for the band, I wanted to be involved. And I graduated from Juilliard and I guess this was the first opportunity. I guess by that time I had been doing some things for…

16.t: Ellington the composer: reaching beyond the form
16.s: Henderson says Ellington's compositions extended street jazz into dramatic forms.
16.q: Okay. Ellington as a composer had a great effect on me because … well first of all, I have to preface this, what I'm gonna tell you now is a result both of hindsight and of foresight. In other words I'm looking back on those days in somewhat more specific form or more than I would have at that…

16.t: Ellington's titles and The Clothed Woman
16.s: He says Ellington's imaginative titles show dramatic content; Holley and Henderson discuss The Clothed Woman as a message not a showpiece.
16.q: Yes, well as a composer I think what his effect mainly has been, two things, that is, that I'm encouraged in using the ethnic expressions, our ethnic expressions in whatever frameworks we happen to find ourselves. I think that that's one of the things that he tried to and did do. And it didn't…

16.t: Take the A Train, Black and Tan Fantasy and All Too Soon
16.s: Henderson comments on four Ellington-associated pieces, including Strayhorn's A Train, the earth sounds of Black and Tan, and Ben Webster in All Too Soon.
16.q: Well so far as what it says about Ellington, it says that he is discriminating and, and happily so in the talents that he chooses to do, to work in, what we used to call Ellingtonia. Billy Strayhorn is such an unusual talent and such an unusual choice, I don't think, I think it will stand in the…

16.t: Ellington composing on the orchestra and the meaning of Harlem
16.s: Ellington wrote on his orchestra for specific players and messages; Harlem portrays all facets of black life.
16.q: Oh well, what's my reaction to that? That is, that's the description of who and what Ellington was and what his composition … he composes on the orchestra, on his orchestras, not with or for. That's what I think that is.

16.t: His role as Ellington's symphonic arm
16.s: He explains how he adapted Ellington's sound for a symphonic setting while staying faithful to it.
16.q: Well it's more what, where did I bring the Ellington sound, the Ellington sound is the nucleus of everything. Now what did I do with it. I embroidered upon it to the extent that it could be put in the setting of the symphonic concert hall. Now how did we do that. We do that by assuming that this…

16.t: Orchestrating Indiana, New World A-Comin', Harlem and Three Black Kings
16.s: He describes adding symphonic forces to Ellington works, the recordings, and his fuller arrangement of Three Black Kings for Dance Theater of Harlem.
16.q: All right. Well this was one of my favorite jazz pieces and it happened to be a standard and it was one of those that I did during that one week that I first joined Ellington for dance music.

16.t: Night Creature for Don Gillis at Carnegie Hall
16.s: In 1955 he orchestrated Duke's Night Creature for the Symphony of the Air, working from taped sketches made while following Ellington on tour.
16.q: Okay. Now I had been a few years away from Lena Horne because I was with her in late '40s, maybe '50s, something like that. Anyway, the Symphony of the Air, Don Gillis had, I don't know, been commissioned that he was to do these works which he was already doing with his band. I don't know if he was…

16.s: He judges Ellington by his own ethnic tradition rather than classical standards, and says Ellington absorbed everyone he heard.
16.q: Not in the proper context at all. Ask about Ellington as a pianist, you have to again decide in what context. If we say in the classical tradition of piano such as that from which has sprung a Horowitz or anybody like that, we would have to say that he's a very poor pianist. But if we say here's a…

16.s: Ellington was always on, teasing him about writing too many notes in his first arrangement.
16.q: Off the bandstand? Oh gosh, suave, debonair, just as he is on. He was always on, I think, in a way of speaking. His more serious moments, I don't know, I would see when he would be, we would be discussing what, how something, how he wanted to do something. Even then he was always a little, what's…

16.t: The A Drum Is a Woman session
16.s: He describes Ellington's one-take recording style and his arrangements for the album.
16.q: Arranger. If I'm listed it’s as an arranger. I remember one was “You'd Better Know It” is one. There was another one but I can't remember exactly what it was. You'd Better Know It. Ozzie Bailey, one of the things that Ozzie Bailey sang, I think, I did a couple and Strayhorn did a couple for Ozzie.…

230.t: The 1972 argument with Ellington about emotion in music
230.s: Barnet recalls a spirited dressing-room discussion at the Grove where Duke said music has no place for emotion and Barnet disagreed, citing Paul Gonsalves at Newport.
230.ch: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
230.q: No, I believe that he -- at that point in his life, I believe that he really believed what he was saying. Now, there may have been a question of semantics, semantics involved there. Because as I recall I agreed with him on this point. I said a person that gets overly emotional and gets high, I…

230.t: Whether Ellington meant it and how the band had changed
230.s: Barnet thinks Duke believed it, noting his age and the changed band after Hodges and Strayhorn.
230.ch: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
230.q: If you get overly exuberant in your playing, you get excited, you have a tendency to maybe over-estimate your ability and attempt things that you wouldn't normally attempt. On the other hand, I mean, some wonderful things have happened out of things like that.

230.ch: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
230.q: Well, good. Because I'm sure people could have read a lot of things into it that weren't really there, because we weren't really angry at each other.

230.s: Barnet says he knew nearly everyone in Duke's band, and tells how Otto Hardwick kept an unplayed bass saxophone with a mirror to watch the showgirls.
230.ch: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington

230.s: Around 1937 Barnet's band took up Ellington voicings through arranger Andy Gibson, and Juan Tizol brought tunes to rehearsals.
230.ch: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
230.q: Oh, that was along around 1937 there. And I got the guys in the band, I said, "Who can I get who can write me some of this stuff?" You know. And so they got me together with a guy by the name of Andy Gibson. And Andy started writing for us, and of course he was very much influenced by the Ellington…

230.t: Sitting in with Ellington at the Casa Manana in 1943
230.s: Barnet tried to get Ellington's band drunk, then played a whole set in Otto Hardwick's chair, with a finale involving both bands.
230.ch: Sidemen, mixed bands, the Apollo and Lena Horne
230.q: This was at the Casa Manana. In fact I have a picture of that. A picture of me sitting in the Ellington section with Johnny Hodges on one side and Harry Carney on the other and the other guys. The Ellington Band and my band -- Joe Zuka, who had the Casa Manana, I was sort of the house band in…

230.t: Billy Strayhorn and the eight bars Barnet never got
230.s: He remembers Strayhorn's compositions and how he repeatedly asked for just eight bars of an arrangement.
230.ch: Retirement and the future of big bands
230.q: Well, let's see. "Prelude to a Kiss," "Warm Valley," "Chelsea Bridge," "Passion Flower," and a lot of other beautiful things.

230.s: Barnet thinks Strayhorn's delicacy needed Duke's soloists and that he did not care about credit, while Barney Bigard was salty about it.
230.ch: Retirement and the future of big bands
230.q: couldn't have found anybody to interpret what he was doing -- well, you get back to the old thing, the alter ego, the association there. You couldn't tell where one left off and the other started, and without each other -- well, let's put it this way. I doubt very much if we'd have heard much about…

230.t: Playing Ellington's tunes, not his arrangements

230.q: No, we didn't play his arrangements. We played his tunes.

230.t: Meeting Duke Ellington at the Cotton Club
230.s: He met Ellington at the downtown Cotton Club, knew his men first, and found Duke fatherly yet hard to read.
230.ch: Glen Island, early records and Duke Ellington
230.q: And I used to be up there, oh, three or four nights a week. And we got to talking to him, and of course I knew the guys in his band before I knew him, and we became good friends, as good a friend as anybody was ever able to be with Duke. Now, Duke, God bless him, he's a wonderful man, but very few…

230.t: Correcting the Ellington myths: Ring Them Bells chimes and the maracas date
230.s: Barnet denies ever playing chimes on Ellington's Ring Them Bells, but says he played maracas on a 1937 Barney Bigard small-band date at Irving Mills's request for a Latin sound.
230.q: Well, yes. It's one of those things that keeps cropping up in discographies and some of the people that write the books, about the big band era, and it just

167.t: How the Ellington organization found him
167.s: Ellington's people heard him in after-hours places and told him where to come; he sat in with Duke's band and was paid a little.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: You understand? And I'd be playing in there and they'd come there and they'd hear me and they'd tell me where to come the next day if they liked what I was doing.

167.t: A short road trip with Ellington
167.s: When Fred Guy got sick Bunn filled in and went out with Duke upstate and around Connecticut for a short time, not five or six months.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: I don't know. I can't think about it, that I did or not. I know --

167.t: Keeping to himself among the Ellington musicians
167.s: He avoided running around with the band, who chased women, and recalls the pretty women in the show.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: Because I couldn't learn nothing running around with them, because they was full of shit -- full of the devil.

167.t: What Duke Ellington was really like
167.s: Bunn found Duke a nice, alert businessman with common sense who kept people at a distance.
167.ch: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
167.q: That's right. He was alert. He understood everything people were saying. Common sense, in other words.

167.t: What Duke Ellington was like to work for
167.s: Duke was fine, took a few drinks, used no dope, and kept writing music; Bunn learned the arrangements by ear.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: And he'd turn his head to me, you know, where I would come in at. And by me learning what they were playing, I learnt the whole arrangements, man. And I couldn't read a note, but I knew where I was supposed to come in and that's where I was.

167.t: Perfect pitch and being a fill-in man
167.s: He credits his perfect pitch for his reputation and says he filled in what he did not know, which Duke liked.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: Well, see, I've got a perfect ear, perfect pitch. And that's why I am so well know, because I've got perfect pitch. Anything I hear, I play.

167.t: Why he left Ellington: he could not read the charts
167.s: Duke took the big band on the road and offered to take Bunn if he could read, but the notes scared him so he stayed.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: And I told him no. I said, 'I don't think I can cut this.' So he said, 'Well, you think it over and if you want to go we'll take you.' So it come to it that Duke had to go right away, see, so he said, 'I can't wait no longer, Teddy. Do you think you can cut it?' I said, 'I don't think so, Duke.' So…

167.t: Never reading music; how he knew his cues in the orchestra
167.s: He never read notes and learned his place at rehearsal; Duke would look at him when it was his turn to fill in.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: I wouldn't know what a note looked like. I know what they look like, but you know, I wouldn't --

167.t: Staying on with Ellington; Fred Guy and the guitar role
167.s: Duke kept him after his first night; Fred Guy played rhythm banjo while Bunn took fills and solos.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: Not unless he sat in with me and I forgot that.

167.t: No guitar parts existed; how Fred Guy read
167.s: There were no guitar charts for him, so he had to play by ear, while Fred Guy read chord charts on banjo.
167.ch: Harlem, the Cotton Club and Duke Ellington
167.q: I had to do it by ear. If I was going I had to do it by ear, because he didn't have the notes for no guitar, period.

167.t: Bubber Miley at the Cotton Club
167.s: Bunn remembers Bubber Miley as an alcoholic who could read everything Duke wrote; they worked the Cotton Club together.
167.ch: Duke, Eddie Lang and other guitarists
167.q: Yeah. He was strictly an alcoholic, God rest his soul. Yeah. Yeah, I worked the Cotton Club with him, with Duke.

6.t: Leaving Kirby for Duke Ellington's call in 1946
6.s: The Copacabana closed, Kirby was missing for two weeks, and when Duke called, Procope took the job to make up lost time, not expecting to stay 28 years.
6.q: Oh, no, no, no, no, no, no, no. I couldn't take that, you know. And I couldn't -- in other words, doing what he was doing at that time wasn't furthering myself, wasn't in my groove, let's say, because there wasn't too much happening. And after the Copacabana closed, then I don't remember exactly,…

6.t: First impressions of Duke's band from inside
6.s: He rode the bus two or three weeks observing and listening, finding the band different inside than the white-suit public image.
6.q: Well, in a way yes, and in a way, no. You see, when you see something from afar you get one image, and when you know it from within it's another image, which holds for Duke Ellington's band. There were a lot of things that were happening in the band that the general public, you know, when they go…

6.t: Joining Duke for one night: Worcester broadcast, Providence, then the Paramount
6.s: Duke called him to replace Otto Hardwick for a Worcester broadcast and a dance; he was gradually persuaded to stay, was hired after about ten days and asked about pay.
6.q: he called me to play this important Saturday afternoon broadcast in Worcester, Massachusetts. So I went there. I went up to Massachusetts that afternoon and played the broadcast with him, and --

6.t: Toby Hardwick's advice and Hodges on dealing with Duke
6.s: Hardwick, his friend since early days, gave advice about the band, Hodges told him to know what to say to Duke, and Toby later recorded Come Sunday and left the business.
6.q: Well, he just -- he was gone. But Toby -- because Toby was my friend, too, because he was one of the first musicians I met when I first started playing, and he told me. So every time I'd see him, he'd sort of give me advice about the band, you know. He'd say, "Don't let them do this to you, because…

6.t: Billy Strayhorn's brilliance and how he learned to arrange
6.s: Strayhorn joined around 1939 to write lyrics but learned arranging from Duke's scores, becoming one of the best arrangers ever.
6.q: Yeah. Now, Duke Ellington hired Billy Strayhorn to write lyrics. In other words they'd have a team. Duke would write the music and Billy Strayhorn would write the lyrics. Billy Strayhorn was one of the most brilliant men I've ever known. Billy Strayhorn would have been successful, tremendously…

6.t: Strayhorn in Duke's shadow and his freedom and pay
6.s: Strayhorn wasn't frustrated, Procope thinks; he was on salary, earned from songs, and sometimes vanished for months before being given a flood of work.
6.q: And Duke must have paid him -- he probably -- I don't know, but he must have, you know, had a very good contract with Duke, judging from the way he lived and, you know, everything.

6.t: Strayhorn in Paris: speaking French and his piano as his car
6.s: In Paris Strayhorn addressed the audience in French and translated signs for Procope; he was unassuming and said his piano was his car.
6.q: Yeah. And just to show you what kind of a guy Billy was, we went to Paris, and Duke called Billy out on the stage and he addressed the audience in French. He spoke to the audience in French.

6.t: Freedom to write for the band; Mood Indigo 5,000 times
6.s: Duke didn't push composing but would play a member's arrangement if worthy; Procope says every Mood Indigo was a new experience.
6.q: Well, I wouldn't say that he encouraged you, but if you did have a -- you know, if you were inclined that way he wouldn't, you know, stop you. And he'd let you make your arrangement and he'd have the band play it, and if he thought it worthy to play, you know, he'd do it. If he didn't think it was…

6.t: Cliques in the Ellington band? Observing before talking
6.s: Outsiders told him the band had cliques; he joked he must belong to all of them and says you only know people by working with them.
6.q: Well, there's a sort of a little joke about that, because, as I say, people on the outside didn't know what went on on the inside of the band. So the musicians who weren't in the band, you know, all of the musicians about town, they'd say to me, 'Well, how are you getting along?'

6.t: Why he stayed 28 years: Duke kept updating the repertoire
6.s: Duke made some fifteen different arrangements of Solitude and other hits, so playing them never went stale.
6.q: Duke Ellington kept his band and his music up to date. Now, like I was telling some people last night, Duke, he listened to a -- for instance, we have certain tunes which are popular, like take, "Solitude," for instance. During the time I was in the band Duke must have made 15 different…

6.t: Procope declines to discuss Ruth Ellington
6.s: Asked about Ruth's role, he says it is an invasion of privacy and he doesn't care to discuss it.
6.q: Well, that's another story. I don't care to get involved in that, because it won't prove anything. What I have to say about all these things -- I don't think -- to my mind that's an invasion of privacy. I don't mind, you

673.t: What made the Ellington band unique
673.s: Berry and Cooper say Duke was the champ and the band ran unlike any other, with players leaving mid-tune unpunished.
673.q: Or THE. I mean Buster can tell you this, corroborate it or anybody else, everybody from Count Basie on down said, you know, I mean there was no question, Duke was it. He was the champ. And it was not a question of rivalry or anything like that, because Ellington had everything covered hands down.…

673.t: Cooper joins Ellington; the bus wreck and the record date
673.s: Cooper recounts meeting the band in Paris, being called for gigs, and the head-on crash on his first night, followed by a recording date.
673.q: And we were standing out on the highway for hours, and finally an old rickety school bus comes and picks us up, and drives us straight to the record studio. It doesn’t matter that we had a wreck or anything like that, we’d go to the record date and make the record.

673.s: Duke would hand off unfinished tunes to Strayhorn, who returned perfect solutions.
673.q: Or over the phone. “Strayhorn, I’m stuck here, you know with this, do something with it,” and the way the stories go I’m sure it’s true, is Strayhorn would send something out that was like perfect, like as though they were reading each other’s minds.

673.s: Berry and Cooper describe Duke as the brightest person they met, with a halo-like presence.
673.q: The perfect solution, you know. Also, Duke Ellington was the — how do you say this — he was the smartest, brightest person I’ve ever met. Period.

673.t: Ellington's seventieth birthday at the White House
673.s: Berry recalls the spotlight following Ellington among the President and Cabinet.
673.q: Yes. I was at the White House for his seventieth birthday. And there were like not only a bunch of great, world famous jazz musicians, but there was the President, the Vice President, the Cabinet, the Supreme Court and heaven knows who else. And the spotlight was on Ellington at all times. I mean…

673.t: The Ellington band book, Cat Anderson, and no chord changes
673.s: Berry describes unnumbered music, trading his tie for a uniform, Cat Anderson's advice, Duke's 'fix it' attitude, and Cootie's note.
673.q: Well a big band, they have music, right? Written parts. And they number them and title them so you can find what you’re looking for. Not Ellington. The first night that I was

673.q: Yes. It seemed like every time we had a day off or something we were making another record. I mean always. There are still records of Ellington’s that are coming out that I’m on that have never been released yet.

673.t: Good nights and bad nights in the Ellington band
673.s: Chill-bump nights, a bad Chicago ballroom night rescued by Basie's band arriving, and festival slumps.
673.q: I don’t remember. I don’t think it was the Triaon, but the band sounded awful all night. And it was the best band in the world, and also the worst. You know, ying and yang. It would go this high or this low. You know, and the band had been just, nobody gave a

673.s: Woods asks about two Ellington tunes; Berry says audiences recognize the piano intro and applaud.
673.q: The introduction. You don’t even have to get into the melody. You play the piano introduction and everybody starts applauding.

87.t: Duke Ellington wrote for his players and loved his band

87.q: Carney Connie used to tell me stories about Duke. They used to drive, and he said Duke wouldn't like for you to talk, you know, he says, because he's getting his ideas together. He said one reason Duke liked for him to go with him because he kept quite, quiet. He didn't like to talk anyway. Carney…

87.t: Duke visiting Honolulu; music as his life
87.s: Ellington visited Young in Honolulu before his death, marveled that Young used a plunger, and was always composing; Willard describes his portable piano.
87.q: Yeah. He was beautiful though. He came up to where I'm playing in Honolulu about a year or so before he passed, you know. And he was talking to Sally, man, they were up there talking. He said -- you know, he had all the flowery words he used. And I play a few of his songs, "Mood Indigo", you know,…

87.t: Why he never worked with Duke
87.s: Contracts with Raymond Scott and a 52nd Street club kept him from joining Ellington, and club owners paid by name value.
87.q: -- nobody was hearing anything about him until Duke brought him doing these things. I regret that I never worked with Duke, and I had a chance to work with him once. But I -- when he wanted me I couldn't get away. I was tied up. I was tied up around New York at that time. I had some contractual…

87.t: Duke Ellington in a class by himself
87.s: Ellington had hits from his own compositions before any of the others.
87.q: Of course, Duke always did have -- I have to exclude Duke when I talk about big bands and things because Duke to me was in a class by himself always, you know, and I think that's how all of us musicians looked upon Duke, because way back when, before any of us doing anything with recordings, Duke…

87.t: Hearing Duke at the Lincoln Colonnade in Washington
87.s: He heard Ellington's band at dances at the Lincoln Colonnade and got to know the young Ellington men.

87.t: Duke's favorite tune and re-arranging "Come Sunday"
87.s: Ellington grew tired of a finished tune and kept rearranging it, as "Come Sunday" featured Hodges, then Ray Nance and Bunny Briggs.
87.q: Well, you know, what they tell me. 'He never finished a lot of things that he started, a lot of tunes. And he told me himself that once he wrote a tune and they played it, he got tired of it then. He'd want to go on to something else, you know. Well, that's true genius, you know. He can't stay…

87.s: Young says Smith was superstitious in the Lunceford band and grew more so with James and Ellington.

87.t: John Hendricks and the Armstrong-Ellington record
